history.title: Name What You Gave Up

data.body:
**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

Every choice has a price, and the price is usually not money. This week you learn to name the thing you gave up, which is the one question economics is actually about.

1. Read **Everything Has a Cost**.
2. Learn the words in **Choice Words**, then win the **Crossword** and the **Matching** game.
3. Keep the **Every Choice, Two Columns** chart open.
4. Trace **Why Choosing Is Unavoidable** before the quiz.
5. Sort the cards in **Scarce or Just Expensive?**
6. Take **Choice Check**.
7. Lock it in with **Remember the Second Best**.
8. Read **Money Questions Kids Ask**.
9. Finish with **Decide: The Community Centre Hour**.

Your job this week: catch yourself making one real choice and name what you gave up. ⚖️

history.title: Everything Has a Cost
history.data:
## Everything Has a Cost

You have one free hour. You can see friends, finish a project, or sleep. Whatever you pick, you did not do the other two.

That sentence is most of economics.

Economics is often described as being about money. It is really about **scarcity**: there is not enough of something to satisfy every want, so choosing is unavoidable. Time is scarce. Money is scarce. Clean water is scarce in some places and not in others. Even attention is scarce.

Scarcity is not the same as being rare, and it is not the same as being expensive. Something is **scarce** when people want more of it than exists. Sand is cheap and enormously common, and construction sand is genuinely scarce in some regions because demand outruns what can be dug.

Because things are scarce, every choice is a **trade-off**. You gain one thing and give up another.

Economists give the thing you gave up a name: **opportunity** cost. It is not everything you turned down. It is the single **alternative** you would have picked instead — your next best option. If you chose sleep over friends and a project, and you would have chosen friends next, then the opportunity cost of sleeping is seeing your friends. The project does not count. It was third.

That definition sounds fussy and it is the useful part. It forces you to name one specific thing rather than waving at everything.

Opportunity cost also explains decisions that look strange from outside. A town that spends on a new road is not against libraries. It made a choice, and the library was what it gave up. Judging the decision means comparing the **benefit** of the road against the library, not against nothing.

There is a trap worth knowing. Money already spent and not recoverable is a **sunk** cost, and it should not affect what you do next. If you paid for a ticket to a film you now know you will hate, the money is gone whether you go or not. The real choice is only about the next two hours. People find this genuinely hard, and knowing the word does not make it easy.

One more idea. Doing a bit more of something is a **marginal** decision. The question is rarely all or nothing. It is: is one more hour of practice worth what that hour costs me?

So when you meet a decision, yours or a government's, ask two things. What is scarce here? And what exactly got given up?

history.title: Choice Check

questions.question: You could see friends, finish a project, or sleep. You sleep, and friends was your next choice. What is the opportunity cost?
options: Seeing your friends, and only that
The project and the friends together
Nothing, because sleep was free to do
The hour of time that you used up
questions.correctAnswer: Seeing your friends, and only that
questions.conceptLabel: opportunity cost is the next best

questions.question: What does it mean for something to be scarce?
options: It costs a large amount of money to buy
People want more of it than there is
Very little of it exists anywhere on Earth
It can only be found in a few countries
questions.correctAnswer: People want more of it than there is
questions.conceptLabel: scarce is not the same as rare

questions.question: Sand is common and cheap, yet construction sand is scarce in some regions. Why?
options: Because most sand has already been used up
Because sand is far rarer than people realise
Because demand there outruns what can be supplied
Because governments have banned digging for it
questions.correctAnswer: Because demand there outruns what can be supplied
questions.conceptLabel: scarce is not the same as rare

questions.question: You paid for a film ticket and now know you will hate the film. What should the ticket price affect?
options: It should push you to attend, to avoid waste
It should be split evenly across the decision
It should be weighed against the film's length
Nothing, because the money is gone either way
questions.correctAnswer: Nothing, because the money is gone either way

questions.question: A town funds a new road instead of a library. What does opportunity cost say about judging that?
options: Compare the road's benefit against the library's
Judge the road entirely on its own merits alone
Assume the council does not value libraries much
Add both costs together to find the total spent
questions.correctAnswer: Compare the road's benefit against the library's
questions.conceptLabel: opportunity cost is the next best

questions.question: Explain why scarcity, not money, is described as what economics is really about.
questions.expectedAnswer: Scarcity means people want more of something than exists, so choosing is unavoidable. That applies to time, attention, water and space, not just money. Because everything scarce forces a choice, and every choice gives something up, scarcity is the more general idea and money is only one example of it.
questions.conceptLabel: scarce is not the same as rare

questions.question: Describe a real decision you made this week, and name its opportunity cost precisely.
questions.expectedAnswer: Answers vary. A full answer names the option chosen, then names one specific alternative that would have been taken instead, rather than listing everything given up, and explains why that one was the next best.
questions.conceptLabel: opportunity cost is the next best

history.title: Money Questions Kids Ask

data.question: Is anything actually free? 🤔
data.answer: Some things are free of charge. Almost nothing is free of cost, because taking it uses time or attention or space that had another use. A free concert still costs you the evening.

data.question: If I enjoy both options equally, is the cost zero?
data.answer: No, it is high. Opportunity cost is not about regret; it is what you gave up. If the two were nearly equal, you gave up something nearly as good, which is exactly why the choice felt hard. What is small is how much better off you ended up.

data.question: Does this mean money decisions are the only real ones? 💸
data.answer: The opposite. Time is scarce for everyone, including people with plenty of money, which is why a busy person paying for a faster option is behaving perfectly rationally.

data.question: Why do people fall for sunk costs so often?
data.answer: Because walking away feels like admitting waste, and people dislike that more than they dislike losing a further hour. Economists have studied it for decades and knowing the word does not immunise you.

data.question: Is scarcity the same as poverty? ⚖️
data.answer: No. Poverty is not having enough for a decent life, which is a serious problem to solve. Scarcity is the general condition that wants exceed what exists, and it applies to everyone, rich or poor.

data.question: Can a government just make more of something?
data.answer: Sometimes, and always at a cost. Building more housing uses workers and materials that were going to build something else. That is opportunity cost operating at national scale.

history.title: Decide: The Community Centre Hour
history.meta: 7th Grade • Decision brief • one hour, four claimants

data.title: The Community Centre Hour
data.instructions: Four groups want the same hour in the same room. Recommend one, name the opportunity cost precisely, and defend it to the group that loses.
data.fitReason: D2.Eco.2 asks students to evaluate alternatives in terms of benefits and costs. Forcing one recommendation from four claims on a genuinely scarce resource makes opportunity cost something they have to name rather than define.

brief.context: The community centre has one room free on Tuesdays from four to five. Four groups have asked for it: a homework club, a seniors' exercise class, a youth band rehearsal, and a food-bank sorting session. Only one can have it.
brief.audience: All four groups, who will each be told the decision and the reason
brief.drivingQuestion: Which group should get the hour, what exactly is the opportunity cost of that decision, and can you justify it to the group that came second?
brief.seedDirection: Rank all four before you decide. You cannot name an opportunity cost without knowing which one came second.
lockedLessonFacts: Scarcity means people want more of something than exists.
Every choice is a trade-off: you gain one thing and give up another.
Opportunity cost is the single next best alternative, not everything turned down.
Money already spent is a sunk cost and should not shape the next decision.
openQuestions: How do you compare benefits that are not measured in the same units?
Does it matter how many people each group serves, or who they are?
Would your answer change if one group had already bought equipment for that room?
stakeholders: The four groups competing for the hour
The centre staff who must explain the decision
People served by the group that loses
criteria: All four options are ranked, not just the winner named
The opportunity cost is stated as one specific alternative, with a reason it ranked second
At least one benefit that is hard to measure is acknowledged rather than ignored
The sunk-cost question is answered explicitly
At least four glossary words used correctly
constraints: One hour, one room, one group
A decision is required; no splitting the hour
Every claim needs a stated reason
brief.deliverable: A panel decision: the ranked list of four, the recommendation, the opportunity cost named precisely, and a short paragraph addressed to the second-place group explaining the reasoning.

parallelExample.context: A panel gave the hour to the group that had already bought floor mats for that room.
parallelExample.move: Challenged on it, they recognised the mats were a sunk cost, reranked on benefit alone, and changed their answer. They kept a note explaining why the mats had felt so persuasive.
parallelExample.whyItHelps: They caught themselves letting spent money steer a forward-looking decision, which is the exact trap the reading names.

supports.frameStarter: We recommend ____. Our second choice was ____, so the opportunity cost is ____. We say this to them because ____.
coachPrompts: Did you rank all four, or only pick a winner?
Is your opportunity cost one specific thing, or a vague list?
Did any already-spent money sneak into your reasoning?
